title: The Taylor Swift Museum Exhibition Is an SOS Call
text:
When the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, shared Tuesday that it would mount an exhibition of Taylor Swift costumes, instruments, and other objects next year, the public response seemed to fall into two camps. Swifties were thrilled, and art purists criticized the museum for succumbing to visitor bait. But really, neither scorn nor celebration is the right response to a show that one of the museum’s curators describes as representing “a remarkable musical journey across genres over the last 20 years.” A 156-year-old institution raiding a pop star’s closet should be seen for what it is: a cry for help.

 The show does not entirely flout museum norms. The MFA’s collection includes fashion and musical instruments. Art institutions have examined celebrity wardrobes in the past (see the landmark David Bowie exhibition that traveled around the world), and museums frequently highlight living visual artists and designers—sometimes, as in the Met’s recent plans for a John Galliano exhibit, to their peril. Why not Swift? She seems to have conquered nearly every other corner of the culture. An illustration of her range: She both is the subject of university courses and once had her own special-edition ketchup bottle . Perhaps to her fans, her rightful place in history is alongside the old masters and the Impressionists. Step back, and you can see why there’s hype for the show, but it’s still a mismatch.

 The museum sector has been having a hard time lately, making this type of pop-culture play understandably tempting. But after the MFA laid off 33 employees, including curators of Islamic art, Native American art, and fashion arts, earlier this year, the show choice looks more than a little desperate. Although Taylor Swift’s sartorial history may be worthy of serious scholarly analysis—mass culture certainly has a place in art museums, which should help us understand the visual world writ large—tackling the subject of a living celebrity at the height of her fame renders hagiography practically a foregone conclusion. The MFA is not even pretending otherwise: One staffer made a point of extending a special welcome to Swifties in the announcement. The exhibition will very likely serve as an advertisement for a star who needs no such boost in the hopes that the museum can lure more visitors, who will be paying $40 each to look at her stuff.

 For an institution that contains one of the finest art collections in the world, the decision belies a deep insecurity. When I saw the news, I had an urge to shout at the MFA like it’s a friend of mine who’s in a toxic relationship: You don’t need her, buddy! You’re great! 

 The tendency to star-cast museum shows does not necessarily lead to bad or uninteresting results. These exhibitions have historically taken one of two approaches: In one, the celebrity might be drafted to curate an exhibition (which must be a tad annoying to the curators who might’ve gone through the trouble of getting a degree to do that). In the other, the museum assembles an exhibit of the celebrity’s belongings or artistic ephemera.

 The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which went through its own round of layoffs last year, recently opened an exhibition doing a bit of both. The institution is currently showcasing nearly 150 works from the art collection of the BTS member RM, and the show is co-curated by the K-pop star himself. Some celebrity-infused endeavors have succeeded, such as the acclaimed Bowie show or a well-liked exhibition of Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz’s collection that the Brooklyn Museum organized. Others, such as Björk at the Museum of Modern Art in 2015 or the Pablo Picasso show co-curated by Hannah Gadsby at the Brooklyn Museum in 2023, flopped with critics but drew crowds, presumably fulfilling their purpose.

 If it’s not clear, I am neither a Swiftie nor a K-pop stan, which may disqualify me from a conversation for the truly devout. That said, having lived in Seoul, I am a real admirer of Korean art and would accept almost any strategy to show more Americans Kim Whanki’s moving abstractions or Chang Ucchin’s charming pastoral scenes. And the RM exhibit has done that, breaking museum records. Even so, something feels off to me.

 Such shows can raise ethical questions—displaying any person’s art collection, for example, can inflate its value—but more than that, they can hurt a museum’s credibility. A doctor would not hand her sutures over to Beyoncé just because her surgery numbers are down, nor would a losing football team throw Justin Bieber on the field because he might bring in some new fans. The stakes are different in museums, but these places shape history, care for cultural heritage, and at their core, are meant to challenge and educate visitors. The stakes of swapping in celebrities for curators and their paraphernalia for objects are not exactly low either.

 Many museums have struggled to rebound after the pandemic changed visitor habits and have not found their way in a world that seems to become more digital by the day. They’ve faced alternating allegations of being overly woke and being complicit in colonialism. And although they are widely trusted , museums remain one of the few places that spark anxiety among would-be visitors over not having done their homework. No one hesitates to go to a concert because they didn’t study music theory. Perhaps you cannot blame the MFA or SFMOMA for looking to the crowd-pleaser to pad the numbers. It’s easy. Too easy.

 Paying the bills, for the MFA, might mean loosening up a bit—not everyone wants to parse the stories told by an intricate Japanese folding screen or sit long enough with a Mondrian to see how it’s more than just a colorful grid. But museums’ usual purview holds plenty of mass appeal as is. In a way, the situation parallels how museums tap certain go-to artists and genres to woo the public: Yayoi Kusama with her impossibly photogenic mirrors; Impressionists with their coffee-table-book-ready textural landscapes; the treasures of ancient Egypt . The best museums don’t just give people what they want, though; they teach us how to look, and empower us to find aesthetic joy for ourselves.

 More compelling than celebrity shows are efforts to pull new audiences that confidently lean into what museums already do. Many have started opening for late-night hours, becoming the kinds of third places so many communities are short on. The Museum of Vancouver recently went the Brené Brown route and highlighted its vulnerability, giving “austerity tours” that showed the toll of low funding. (Kind of depressing—but it definitely got people talking.) The National Gallery of Art, meanwhile, has a curator translating old objects into the language of Gen Z on social media; the institution is also inviting people in for “Finding Awe” sessions that train visitors to look closely and patiently at objects. During a recent session, a visitor commented that after seeing so much AI content, noticing the imperfections of an Agnes Martin canvas felt rewarding. Museums can make themselves relevant to contemporary viewers by finding the relatable and the universal in the art they’re trusted with stewarding, not borrowing relevance in the shape of a celebrity’s dress.

 A common justification for more populist shows goes something like: The exhibition gets visitors in the door. After that, they might encounter something that could spark a lifelong interest in art . I don’t love the way this logic characterizes art like a bad-tasting pill that must go down coated in peanut butter. The art museum’s job, if nothing else, is to convince us that the art is the peanut butter. So if there must be a Swift show, I hope the thinking proves true. During the Swift exhibit’s run, the MFA will also, at one point, be hosting a show of paintings by Mary Cassatt , the only American to exhibit with the French Impressionists. Cassatt had an intimate and intentional way of capturing women’s experiences in a male-dominated world. Sound familiar? Maybe some of those visiting Swifties will enter their Cassatt era next.
